# Foundations

### What is a *Random Variable*?

- sample space: different possible outcomes associated with a probability
- a random variable *X*, a function that associates to each outcome $\omega \in S$ exactly one number X($\omega$) = $x$ (for example, number of tosses until one gets a head (H))
- $S_{x}$ is all the $x$'s (all the possible values of X, the support of X)

Example: coin tosses till H

- $X: \omega -> x$
- $\omega :$ H, TH, TTH,... (infinite)
- $x = 0,1,2,...; x \in S_{x}$

And $X(\omega)=x$: $H -> 1$, $TH ->2$,...

### Probability Distribution Functions

- every discrete random variable X has associated with it a *probability mass function (PMF)*
- continuous RVs: *probability density functions (PDFs)*
- $px$ : $S_{x}$ , $x \in $S_{x}$ 

**Cumulative distribution function**: cumulative probability of getting a heads in 1 or less, 2 or less tosses,...

### Binomial random variable

- toss coin 10 times, two possible outcomes, number of successes
- FORMULA 

Calculate the probability of P(X <= x), seeing n heads, using cumulative distribution function

```{r}
n <- 10 # sample size
p <- 0.5 # probability of success

probs <- rep(NA, 11)
for (x in 0:10){
    probs[x+1] <- round(pbinom(x, size=n, prob=p), digits=2) 
}

data.frame(p = seq(0,10), p = probs)
```

10 has to be one because it encompasses all possible outcomes (n=10). 
the distribution is cumulative: if 2 heads, you can add probability of getting 0,1 and 2 heads,...

discrete data!


Probability of getting exactly 1 head:
```{r}
choose(10,1) * 0.5 * (1-0.5)^9
dbinom(1, size=10, prob=0.5)
```

Generate random binomial data

```{r}
rbinom(1, n=10, prob=0.5)
```

### Continuous data

- we cannot talk about the probability of each outcome
    - probability density function does not give you the probability of seeing an exact number, i.e. a point value (this is only possible in the discrete case)
    - in the continuous case: we talk about an area under the curve, there's an infinity of possible values between two values (which is different in the discrete case)
    - for example, P(x<1.69)
- the pdf of the normal distribution: $X ~ norm(mean=\mu, sd = \sigma)$

```{r}

plot(function(x) dnorm(x, 0, 1), -3,3,
main = 'Normal density', ylim=c(0,.4),
ylab = 'density', xlab='X')
```

Probability of seeing possible range of values
```{r}
pnorm(Inf) - pnorm(-Inf)
pnorm(2) - pnorm(-2)
pnorm(3) - pnorm(-3)
pnorm(0.5) - pnorm(-0.5)
```

Quantiles: what is the value (quantile $x$) of a $Normal(\mu, \sigma)$ such that $P(X<x)=0.975$. 

```{r}
qnorm(0.975, mean=500, sd=100)
```

It is also possible to compute upper tail:

```{r}
pnorm(2, lower.tail=T)
pnorm(2, lower.tail=F)
1- pnorm(2, lower.tail=T)
```

Overview of functions:

- dnorm: the pdf
- pnorm: the cdf
- qnorm: the inverse of cdf
- for binomial: dbinom, pbinom, qbinom
- for t-distribution: dt, pt, qt 

### Maximum Likelihood Estimation

- sample mean (xbar), standard deviation (sd)
    - MLE of the true underlying distribution that we don't know
- joint probability of getting all these values
    - because they are independent: we can multiply all of the probabilities
    - the probability is a function of $\theta$, this is the likelihood function
    - $\theta$ is the only variable that stays the same

#### Discrete case
```{r}
x <- c(5,4,3,5,2)
theta <- seq(0,1,by=0.01)
store <- rep(NA, length(theta))
for(i in 1:length(theta)){
    store[i] <- prod(dbinom(x, size=10, prob=theta[i]))
}

plot(density(store))

```

- maximum value on curve =  MLE
- in the case of the binomial: $\theta = x$ divided by $n$
- in the *Continuous case*: sample mean and variance will give you MLE

**Significance of the MLE**

- having assumed a particular pdf, we can estimate the (unknown) parameters (mean and variance) of the distribution that generated our particular data -> distributional properties of the mean under repeated sampling

```{r}
abs(qt(0.025, df=15))

```
